en: The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra Spoken by Mañjuśrī,
Volume One,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Mandarakaśyapa of Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

These were all adorned with the great adornments and had already attained the stage of non-retrogression. Their names were Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Unhindered Eloquence Bodhisattva, and Not Abandoning the Burden Bodhisattva; he was accompanied by such great bodhisattvas as these.
When the first light of dawn appeared, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta came from his own abode to the place where the Buddha was and stood outside.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, and other such great śrāvakas, each departed from their respective residences and went together to where the Buddha was, standing outside.
When the Buddha knew that the assembly had all gathered, the Tathāgata emerged from his dwelling, prepared a seat, and sat down.
He addressed Śāriputra:
"For what reason are you standing outside the gate at this early hour?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has already arrived here and is standing outside the gate.”
"I actually arrived late in the evening.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Mañjuśrī,
"Did you truly arrive at this dwelling place first, wishing to see the Tathāgata?"
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
I have indeed come here wishing to see the Tathāgata.”
Why is this? Because I delight in right contemplation for the benefit of sentient beings.

I contemplate the Tathāgata as the mark of suchness (*tathatā*), not a differentiating mark; a mark of immovability, a mark of non-action; a mark of non-arising, a mark of non-ceasing; a mark of neither existence nor non-existence; a mark of neither being in a direction nor departing from a direction; neither belonging to the three periods of time nor not belonging to them; neither a dualistic mark nor a non-dualistic mark; and neither a defiled mark nor a pure mark.
"By means of such [insights], one correctly contemplates the Tathāgata’s benefit for sentient beings.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If one can see the Tathāgata in this way, the mind neither grasps nor does it not grasp; it is neither an accumulation nor a non-accumulation."
At that time, Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
“If one can see the Tathāgata in the manner you have described, it is truly rare.”
One beholds the Tathāgata for the sake of all sentient beings, yet the mind does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings;
one transforms all sentient beings toward nirvāṇa, yet likewise does not grasp at the mark of nirvāṇa;
one undertakes the great adornment for the sake of all sentient beings, yet the mind does not perceive the mark of adornment.
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī said to Śāriputra:
“So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”
Although they give rise to the mind of great adornment for the sake of all sentient beings, they never perceive the mark of a sentient being;
and although they give rise to the great adornment for the sake of all sentient beings, the realms of sentient beings neither increase nor decrease.

Suppose a single Buddha remains in the world for an eon or more than an eon; and suppose that in this same Buddha-world there are further immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each of whom preaches the Dharma day and night without a moment’s rest for an eon or more than an eon, each delivering immeasurable beings—numerous as the sands of the Ganges—into nirvana, yet the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.

Even so it is throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions; each and every Buddha preaches the Dharma and teaches, delivering immeasurable beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of whom enter nirvana, yet there is neither increase nor decrease in the realm of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because a fixed characteristic of sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.
Śāriputra spoke again to Mañjuśrī, saying:

“If the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases, for what reason do bodhisattvas seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings and constantly practice the preaching of the Dharma?”

Mañjuśrī said: "If all sentient beings were entirely characterized by emptiness, there would likewise be no bodhisattva seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor would there be any sentient beings for whom one might preach the Dharma."
"Why is this? Because within the Dharma that I teach, there is not a single dharma that can be apprehended.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"If there are no sentient beings, how can one speak of the existence of sentient beings and the realm of sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied,
"The characteristic of the realm of sentient beings is like that of the realm of all Buddhas."
He asked again:
"Is the realm of sentient beings finite?
He replied:
“The measure of the realm of sentient beings is like the measure of the realm of the Buddhas.
The Buddha asked again:
“Does the measure of the realm of sentient beings have a location?”
He replied,
"The measure of the realm of sentient beings is inconceivable.
He asked again:
“Does the characteristic of the realm of sentient beings abide?
He replied, “Sentient beings do not abide; they abide like space.”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“When practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this manner, how should one abide in the perfection of wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"To dwell by means of the dharma of non-dwelling is to dwell in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The Buddha again asked Mañjuśrī:
"In what way is 'non-dwelling in dharmas' called dwelling in the perfection of wisdom?"
Mañjuśrī said: “By means of the mark of non-abiding, one abides in the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha again addressed Mañjuśrī:
“When one abides thus in the *prajñāpāramitā*, how do these roots of goodness increase?
How do they diminish? Mañjuśrī replied:
"If one can abide thus in the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is neither increase nor decrease among the roots of goodness, and likewise, there is neither increase nor decrease among all phenomena."
The nature and characteristics of this Prajñāpāramitā are likewise neither increasing nor decreasing,
World-Honored One!
Cultivating Prajñāpāramitā in this manner does not abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings, nor does it grasp at the dharmas of the noble ones.

Why is this? Because in the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not perceive any dharma that can be grasped or abandoned; practicing the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, one likewise does not perceive Nirvāṇa as something to be delighted in, nor saṃsāra as something to be loathed.
Why is this? Because they do not perceive birth and death, how much less could they feel weary of them;
because they do not perceive nirvana, how much less could they take pleasure in or cling to it.

Practicing the perfection of wisdom in this way, one does not perceive any defilements or afflictions to be abandoned, nor does one perceive any merits to be grasped; regarding all phenomena, the mind neither increases nor decreases.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive any increase or decrease within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu),
World-Honored One.
If one can act in this way, it is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
World-Honored One!
Not perceiving that any phenomena have arising or ceasing is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
“World-Honored One!
Not perceiving that any dharmas have increase or decrease—this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
World-Honored One!”
When the mind has no desire for acquisition and does not perceive any dharma-characteristic as something to be sought, this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
World-Honored One!
Not seeing beauty or ugliness, not giving rise to notions of high or low, and not engaging in taking or rejecting—this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because dharmas have neither beauty nor ugliness, as they are free from all marks;
dharmas have neither high nor low, as they are equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
"The Dharma is without taking or rejecting, for it abides in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
This is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“Are these Buddha-dharmas not supreme?
Mañjuśrī replied,
“I do not perceive any dharma that possesses the characteristic of being superior.”
"The Tathāgata has personally realized that all dharmas are empty;
this can be known through realization. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "So it is, so it is!"
"The Tathāgata, through perfect awakening, has personally realized the dharma of emptiness.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In this dharma of emptiness, can any distinction of superiority or inferiority be found?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Mañjuśrī! Is that which you have spoken the true Dharma?
The Buddha spoke again to Mañjuśrī:
"Is 'Anuttara' (Unsurpassed) called the Buddha-dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"As the Buddha has taught, 'Anuttara' is indeed called the Buddha-dharma."
"Why is this? Because there is no dharma that can be named 'Anuttara'. Mañjuśrī said:

"To practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner is not called being a vessel for the Dharma; it is neither a teaching for transforming ordinary beings, nor is it a Buddha-dharma, nor a dharma of increase—this is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not perceive any dharma that can be analyzed or contemplated.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do you not contemplate the Buddha-dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied, "No,
World-Honored One."

As I contemplate it, I do not perceive the Buddha-dharma, nor can one differentiate whether it is the dharma of ordinary beings, the dharma of śrāvakas, or the dharma of pratyekabuddhas; such is called the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not perceive the marks of ordinary beings, does not perceive the marks of the Buddha-dharma, and does not perceive any fixed marks in all phenomena; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive the desire realm, does not perceive the form realm, does not perceive the formless realm, and does not perceive the realm of cessation.
Why is this? It is because not perceiving any dharma as having the characteristic of exhaustion or cessation is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, when cultivating the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive a benefactor nor a recipient of benefit; contemplating these two aspects with a mind free from discrimination is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not perceive any Buddha-dharma to be grasped, nor does one perceive any dharma of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) to be abandoned; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not perceive any dharma of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) that can be extinguished, nor does one perceive any dharma of a Buddha while realizing it with the mind; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!

You are able to thus skillfully explain the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. This is the Dharma-seal in which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train; even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, whether in training or beyond training, should likewise not depart from this seal when cultivating the fruits of the path.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“If there are those who, upon hearing this Dharma, are neither startled nor afraid, they have not merely planted various roots of goodness under a thousand Buddhas; rather, it is only after having long planted the foundations of virtue under hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas that they can remain neither startled nor terrified by this profound Prajñāpāramitā.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall now further explain the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said, “Speak then.
“World-Honored One! [he replied.]

When practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive any dharma as something to be dwelled in or not to be dwelled in, nor does one perceive any objective sphere characterized by grasping or abandoning. Why is this?

Just as all Tathāgatas do not perceive the marks of the objective realm of any phenomena, and do not even perceive the realm of the Buddhas, how much less would they grasp the realms of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or ordinary beings?

One does not grasp at the mark of the conceivable, nor does one grasp at the mark of the inconceivable; one does not perceive that all phenomena possess various marks, for one personally realizes that the dharma of emptiness is inconceivable.

In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have all made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas and planted various roots of goodness; only then are they able to be neither startled nor terrified by this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, when practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, one perceives neither bondage nor liberation; yet, regarding ordinary beings up to those of the three vehicles, one does not perceive any marks of differentiation—this is the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“How many Buddhas have you already made offerings to?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“I and all Buddhas are like illusory transformations; I see neither the offering nor the recipient.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, “Do you now not abide in the Buddha-vehicle?”
Mañjuśrī said, “As I contemplate it, I do not perceive even a single dharma; how, then, could one abide in the Buddha-vehicle?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! Have you not attained the Buddha-vehicle? Mañjuśrī replied:
"The Buddha-vehicle is merely a name; it cannot be obtained, nor can it be seen.
How then could I obtain it?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! Have you attained unimpeded wisdom? Mañjuśrī replied:
"I am myself unimpeded; how can that which is unimpeded attain non-obstruction?
The Buddha said, "Have you sat upon the site of enlightenment?"
Mañjuśrī said, “Since all Tathāgatas do not sit upon the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), how could I alone now sit upon the site of enlightenment?
For what reason? [Because]...”
"Because one directly perceives that all phenomena abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The Buddha asked:
"What is called the 'limit of reality'?"
Mañjuśrī said: "The view of a self-identity and so forth are the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The Buddha said:
“What is the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)? Mañjuśrī replied:
“The view of a self-identity is like the mark of suchness; it is neither real nor unreal, neither coming nor going, and it is both a body and not a body—this is called the limit of reality.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one has attained definitive and thorough understanding of this meaning, such a person is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
"Why is this? Because upon hearing the characteristics of such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds are not startled, not terrified, do not sink, and do not regret.
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To hear such a Prajñāpāramitā, which is complete in its dharma-characteristics, is to be near the seat of the Buddha. Why is this?
"Because the Tathāgata has realized the characteristics of these dharmas.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If one hears this profound Prajñāpāramitā and is able to be neither startled nor terrified, neither discouraged nor regretful, it should be known that such a person is seeing the Buddha.
At that time, there was also the laywoman Animitta who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Whether they be the dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, or the dharmas of buddhas—all these dharmas are without marks.”
Therefore, regarding the Prajñāpāramitā from which one hears it, one shall in all cases neither be startled nor terrified, neither sink into despondency nor feel regret. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are fundamentally without marks.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If good sons and good daughters, upon hearing such a profound Prajñāpāramitā, attain certainty in their minds and are neither startled nor terrified, neither submerged nor regretful."
It should be known that such a person dwells in the stage of non-retrogression.
If a person hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and is neither startled nor terrified, but listens with faith and joy, receiving it with delight and without weariness;

This is the fulfillment of the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā; furthermore, one is able to reveal and analyze them for others, practicing according to what has been taught.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“By what principle do you perceive that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
or that one abides in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
Mañjuśrī said: "I have not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor do I abide in the Buddha-vehicle; how then could I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"What I have spoken is precisely the characteristic of bodhi.
The Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You are able to skillfully explain this meaning within this most profound Dharma.
You have long planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas, and you have cultivated the holy life through the dharma of signlessness."

Mañjuśrī said: "If one perceives signs, then one speaks of signlessness; yet I now perceive neither signs nor signlessness. How, then, can you say that one purifies the holy life by means of the dharma of signlessness?"
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you perceive the precepts of the śrāvakas?
He replied:
“I see it,” [he replied]. The Buddha asked,
“How do you see it?”

Mañjuśrī said: "I do not form the view of an ordinary person, nor do I form the view of a noble one; I do not form the view of one in training, nor the view of one beyond training; I do not form the view of greatness, nor the view of smallness; I do not form the view of the disciplined, nor the view of the undisciplined; I neither see nor do I not see."
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
“If you now view the Śrāvaka-yāna in this manner, how would you view the Buddha-yāna?”
Mañjuśrī said: “I do not perceive the dharma of bodhi, nor do I perceive one who practices for bodhi or one who realizes bodhi.
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī:
"What is meant by 'Buddha,' and how does one contemplate the Buddha? Mañjuśrī replied:
"What is meant by 'self'?
Śāriputra replied, "The 'self' exists only as a name; the characteristic of a name is empty."
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, so it is!
Just as I exist only as a name, so too does the Buddha exist only as a name."
The emptiness of the characteristics of names is itself bodhi; one does not seek bodhi by means of names.
The characteristic of bodhi is beyond words and beyond explanation. Why is this?
To speak of awakening is for both are empty.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, you asked:
[Why do you say that?]"
As for the question, "What is called a Buddha?
How does one contemplate a Buddha?"—that which is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither name nor mark: this is called a Buddha.
"Just as one contemplates the true reality of one's own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha; only the wise are able to know this, and this is called 'contemplating the Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As Mañjuśrī has explained, this Prajñāpāramitā is not something that can be fully understood by a bodhisattva who is a beginner.
Mañjuśrī said, "It is not only a beginner bodhisattva who cannot know it; even those of the two vehicles who have already accomplished what was to be done are likewise unable to understand it."
When the Dharma is expounded in this manner, there is no one who can know it. Why is this?

Because the characteristic of bodhi is that, in reality, there is no dharma that can be known; it is without seeing and without hearing, without attainment and without thought, without arising and without ceasing, and without speaking and without listening.
"In this way, the nature and characteristics of bodhi are empty and quiescent; there is neither realization nor cognition, neither form nor mark.
How, then, could there be one who attains bodhi? Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī, "Does the Buddha not realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the dharma-realm?"
Mañjuśrī said: “No, Śāriputra! Why is that?
The World-Honored One is the dharma-realm.
If one were to use the dharma-realm to realize the dharma-realm, that would constitute a contentious dispute. Śāriputra!
The characteristic of the dharma-realm is itself bodhi. Why is this?
Because within this dharma-realm there is no mark of a sentient being, for all dharmas are empty.
The emptiness of all phenomena is itself bodhi, because it is non-dual and without discrimination.

Śāriputra, within non-discrimination there is no knower; where there is no knower, there is no verbal expression. The characteristic of being beyond verbal expression is neither existence nor non-existence, neither knowing nor not knowing.
All dharmas are likewise thus.
Why is this? Because all dharmas have no location, due to their definitive nature.
The characteristics of such a grave offense are inconceivable. Why is this?
Because the true reality of all phenomena (dharmas) is indestructible.
Likewise, this heinous crime has no intrinsic nature; it is not born in the heavens, nor does it fall into hell, nor does it enter nirvana.
Why is this? All karmic conditions abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); they neither come nor go, being neither cause nor effect.
Why is this? Because the dharma-realm is boundless, having neither beginning nor end.
Therefore, Śāriputra!

If one sees that a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense does not fall into hell, and a practitioner of pure conduct does not enter nirvāṇa, then such a bhikṣu is neither worthy of offerings nor unworthy of offerings, neither one who has exhausted outflows nor one who has not exhausted outflows.
"Why is this? Because one abides in equanimity toward all phenomena.
Śāriputra said:
“What is called ‘the patience of non-retrogression’? Mañjuśrī replied,
“Not perceiving even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of arising or ceasing is called the patience of non-retrogression.”
Śāriputra asked,
“What is meant by a monk who is not disciplined? Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Arhat whose outflows are exhausted is called ‘the untamed. Why is this?
Because all fetters have been extinguished and there is nothing further to be tamed, he is therefore called ‘the untamed.’”
If one's mental activities exceed [the proper measure], they are called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Why is this?
Because ordinary beings do not accord with the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it is called "exceeding."
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, excellent!
You have now skillfully explained for me the meaning of 'Arhat' as one whose outflows are exhausted."
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, so it is!
I am indeed a true Arhat whose outflows are exhausted."

Why is this? Because they have severed the desire for the vehicle of the śrāvaka and the desire for the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha; by these causes and conditions, they are called "Arhats who have attained the destruction of the outflows.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"When the bodhisattvas sit upon the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), do they awaken to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"When bodhisattvas sit upon the site of enlightenment, there is no awakening to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? Because, according to the nature of bodhi, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Since bodhi is signless, who could sit upon it, and who could rise from it?
"For this reason, one does not see a bodhisattva sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), nor does one perceive the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Awakening is the five heinous crimes, and the five heinous crimes are awakening.
Why is this? Because awakening and the five heinous crimes are without two distinct characteristics.

The absence of one who has nothing more to learn and the absence of the state of having nothing more to learn; the absence of seeing and the absence of one who sees; the absence of knowing and the absence of one who knows; the absence of conceptualization and the absence of one who conceptualizes—such characteristics as these are called bodhi.
Seeing the signs of the five heinous crimes is likewise so.
If one says they see bodhi and take it as a realization, you should know that such people are those of overweening pride (adhimāna).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"When you say, 'I am the Tathāgata,' do you mean that I am the Tathāgata?"
Mañjuśrī said: “No, World-Honored One!
Do I not consider that it is not the Tathāgata who is the Tathāgata?”
There is no characteristic of suchness that can be named "suchness," nor is there any Tathāgata-wisdom capable of knowing suchness.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata and wisdom are without dual characteristics.
"Emptiness is the Tathāgata; it exists as nothing more than a name. How then could I say that this is the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, "Do you doubt the Tathāgata?"
Mañjuśrī said: “No, World-Honored One!
I observe that the Tathāgata has no determinate nature; being without birth and without cessation, I have no doubt.”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you not now say that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world? Mañjuśrī replied:
"If a Tathāgata appears in the world, the entire dharma-realm should likewise appear.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"Do you think that the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have entered nirvāṇa?"
Mañjuśrī said, “The Buddhas have a single characteristic, which is inconceivable.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"So it is, so it is! The Buddha is of a single characteristic, the inconceivable characteristic.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Does the Buddha still abide in the world now?
The Buddha spoke to Mañjuśrī:
"So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī said:
"If the Buddha dwells in the world, then Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges should also dwell in the world."
Why is this? All Buddhas are of one and the same characteristic, the inconceivable characteristic.
The inconceivable characteristic is without arising and without cessation.
If all future Buddhas shall appear in the world, then all Buddhas likewise appear in the world.
Why is this? Because within the inconceivable, there are no marks of past, future, or present.
"However, sentient beings cling to them, claiming there is a 'transcending the world' and claiming there is a 'parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"This is what is understood by Tathāgatas, Arhats, and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas."
"Why is this? Because these three kinds of people, upon hearing the profound Dharma, are able neither to slander it nor to praise it.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding such an inconceivable Dharma, who would disparage it?
Who would praise it?”

are ordinary persons also inconceivable?

"Why is this? Because the inconceivable dharma is itself nirvana; they are equal and without distinction. Mañjuśrī said:

Mañjuśrī replied:

The Buddha said,

Mañjuśrī said: “One who wishes to cause the Tathāgata to attain the inconceivable dharma does so while remaining without accomplishment regarding any dharmas.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do you wish for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma and transform beings?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha, "I do wish for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma and transform beings; yet both that which is preached and the one who listens are unattainable."
Why is this? Because they abide in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
There is no distinction between the dharma-realm and sentient beings.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you wish for the Tathāgata to be the unsurpassed field of merit?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Tathāgata is an inexhaustible field of merit; he is of an inexhaustible nature. This inexhaustible nature is the unsurpassed field of merit.
It is neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit; it is called a ‘field of merit.’”
Being devoid of such characteristics as light and darkness, arising and ceasing, and so forth, this is called the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
If one can understand the characteristics of the field of merit in this way, then even when planting seeds of goodness deeply, there will be neither increase nor decrease.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“In what way does planting a seed neither increase nor decrease?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“The characteristics of the field of merit are inconceivable.
If a person cultivates goodness therein in accordance with the Dharma, that too is inconceivable.
To plant seeds in such a manner is called ‘neither increasing nor decreasing,’ and it is also the unsurpassed, most excellent field of merit.”
At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the great earth shook in six ways, manifesting the signs of impermanence.

Sixteen thousand people all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); seven hundred bhikṣus, three thousand upāsakas, forty thousand upāsikās, and sixty billion nayutas of devas from the six heavens of the desire realm were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

Why do you say that one enters the inconceivable samādhi?
When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I wished to enter this concentration; yet now, upon reflection, I realize that there is actually no mental state through which one enters samādhi.
It is like a person learning archery: through long practice they become skillful, so that later, even without conscious intent, their arrows invariably hit the mark because of that long training.

I am also like this: when first learning the inconceivable samādhi, I bind my mind to a single object; once this is accomplished through long practice, there is no further mental activity, and I am constantly in a state of meditative concentration.
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,

Mañjuśrī replied:

Śāriputra asked,
"Is it that the inconceivable concentration cannot be apprehended?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Concentration that is conceivable has the characteristic of being obtainable;
concentration that is inconceivable has the characteristic of being unobtainable.
All sentient beings truly accomplish inconceivable concentration.”
Why is this? Because all mental characteristics are themselves not mind; therefore, it is called the inconceivable samādhi.
For this reason, the characteristics of all sentient beings and the characteristics of the inconceivable samādhi are equal and without distinction.
The Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying:

If one dwells within the perception of existence or the notion of a self, then the *prajñāpāramitā* would have a locus.
If the *prajñāpāramitā* dwells in non-existence, that too is the notion of a self, and it is likewise called a locus.
Departing from these two states, one dwells in non-dwelling, abiding as all Buddhas abide: peacefully established in cessation, a realm beyond conceptual thought.
Such inconceivability is called the dwelling place of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In the locus of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all phenomena are without marks (*animitta*) and all phenomena are without activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

The *prajñāpāramitā* is itself the inconceivable; the inconceivable is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); the dharma-realm is without marks; that which is without marks is the inconceivable; and the inconceivable is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Prajñāpāramitā and the dharmadhātu are non-dual and without distinction.
That which is non-dual and without distinction is the dharmadhātu; the dharmadhātu is signlessness (animitta); signlessness is the realm of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The realm of prajñāpāramitā is the inconceivable realm; the inconceivable realm is the realm of neither arising nor ceasing; and the realm of neither arising nor ceasing is the inconceivable realm.
Mañjuśrī said: "The realm of the Tathāgata and my own realm are non-dual in nature.
One who cultivates the prajñāpāramitā in this manner does not seek for enlightenment."
Why is this? Because the characteristic of awakening is detached, and that is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),

If one knows the mark of self yet does not cling to it—this absence of knowledge and absence of clinging is what the Buddha knows.
This inconceivable absence of knowledge and absence of clinging is precisely what the Buddha knows.
Why is this? Because one knows that the essential nature of the body has no marks of existence.
How, then, could it transform the dharma-realm?
If one knows that the fundamental nature is without substance and without attachment, it is called "non-thing.
If there is no thing, there is no location; it is without support and without abiding.

To be without support and without dwelling is to be without arising and without cessation; to be without arising and without cessation is precisely the merit of both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
If one knows thus, then there is no conceptual mind.
For one who is without mental conceptions, how can they know the conditioned and unconditioned merits?

Such non-knowing is itself the inconceivable; this inconceivability is that which is known by the Buddha. It is neither grasping nor non-grasping; it does not perceive the signs of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—and it does not grasp at arising and ceasing or any formative activities, nor is it characterized by annihilation or permanence.
To know in this way is called right knowledge.
Inconceivable knowledge is like space: it is neither "this" nor "that," it cannot be compared, it is without good or evil, it is beyond equal or unequal, and it is without marks or features.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
“If one knows in this way, it is called non-retrogressive wisdom. Mañjuśrī said:
“Non-active wisdom is called non-retrogressive wisdom; it is like a gold ingot, which must first be struck with a hammer before its quality can be known.
If it were not treated by such striking, no one would be able to know it.”
The characteristics of non-retrogressive wisdom are likewise thus.
It manifests only when one acts within the sphere of experience without recollecting or clinging, without arising or contriving, fully possessing immovability, and neither being born nor ceasing.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“If the Tathāgatas were to speak of their own wisdom themselves, who would be able to believe it?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"In this way, such a wise one possesses neither the dharma of nirvāṇa nor the dharma of saṃsāra; this is the practice of quiescence, this is the practice of immovability. It does not involve the severing of greed, hatred, and delusion, yet it is also not a non-severing."

Why is this? Because it is neither exhausted nor extinguished; it is neither separate from birth and death nor not separate from them; it is neither the cultivation of the path nor the non-cultivation of the path.
One who forms such an understanding is said to possess right faith.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, “Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said;

The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

For example, it is like a householder who, having lost a maṇi jewel, is filled with sorrow and distress;

In the same way, Kāśyapa!
It is the same for bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; they likewise possess a mind of faith and joy.

Neither a place nor a non-place of practice, they all enter into the One Vehicle, which is called the "non-place of practice. Why is this?
Because it is without thought and without action.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should one practice in order to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī! By practicing according to what is taught in the Prajñāpāramitā, one can swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Furthermore, there is the Ekavyūha Samādhi; if a son of good family or a daughter of good family cultivates this samādhi, they will also swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
what is meant by the ‘samādhi of one practice’?”
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma-realm is of a single characteristic; to bind one's conditions to the Dharma-realm is called the Samādhi of One Practice.

If good men or good women wish to enter the Samādhi of One Practice, they must first hear the Prajñāpāramitā and practice and study according to its teachings; only then can they enter the Samādhi of One Practice."
As with the conditions of the dharma-realm, it is non-retrogressive, indestructible, inconceivable, unimpeded, and signless.

Good sons and good daughters who wish to enter the Samādhi of One Practice should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and refrain from grasping at appearances; they should bind their minds to a single Buddha, single-mindedly reciting that name.

Following the direction of the Buddha, with body upright and facing him directly, one can maintain a continuous succession of thoughts upon a single Buddha; within that very mindfulness, one is able to see all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

Why is this? The merit of recollecting a single Buddha is immeasurable and boundless; it is no different from the merit of immeasurable Buddhas. The inconceivable Buddha-dharma is equal and without distinction; all ride upon the same Suchness (tathatā), having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, and are fully endowed with immeasurable merit and immeasurable eloquence.
One who thus enters the Samādhi of One Practice fully knows that the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and the dharma-realm are without any marks of differentiation.

Although the Buddha-dharma heard by Ānanda has enabled him to attain the dhāraṇī of mindfulness and the most excellent eloquence and wisdom among the śrāvakas, he still dwells within the realm of numerical calculation and is therefore subject to limitations and obstructions.
If one attains the Samādhi of One Practice, one will discern each and every dharma-gate of all the sutras, understanding them all completely with certainty and without obstruction.
Day and night one shall constantly preach, and one's wisdom and eloquence will never be exhausted.
Compared to Ānanda’s vast learning and eloquence, even a hundred thousandth part would not equal his.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should form this thought:
"How shall I attain the inconceivable merit and immeasurable renown of the *ekavyūha-samādhi*?"
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should keep the *ekavyūha-samādhi* in mind, constantly applying diligent effort without indolence.

By practicing and training in this sequence, one will gradually be able to enter the *ekavyūha-samādhi* and realize its inconceivable merit. However, those who slander the True Dharma and lack faith, or those hindered by the heavy karmic offenses of evil deeds, cannot enter it.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
It is like a person who obtains a maṇi jewel and shows it to a jeweler.
The jeweler replies:"
"This is a priceless, genuine mani-jewel.
He then requested of his teacher, saying,
"Please polish it for me, so that its luster and color are not lost."
"Once the jewel master has finished polishing it, as he grinds it, the color and radiance of the jewel will shine through from both sides. Mañjuśrī!

If there are good sons or good daughters who cultivate and study the inconceivable merit and immeasurable renown of the Single Practice Samādhi, then as they practice and study, they will know the characteristics of all dharmas, attain clear and unobstructed penetration, and their merit will increase in exactly the same way."
Mañjuśrī! Just as the orb of the sun, with its radiance pervading everywhere, has no sign of diminution;
so too it is when one attains the Samādhi of Single Practice—one becomes fully endowed with all merits, without any deficiency whatsoever.
It illuminates the Buddha-dharma like the light of the solar orb. "Mañjuśrī!
All the teachings I have expounded are of a single flavor, free from flavors—the flavor of liberation, the flavor of quiescent extinction."

If a son or daughter of good family attains this Samādhi of the Single Practice, whatever they expound will likewise be of a single flavor, a flavor free from flavors—the flavor of liberation, the flavor of quiescent extinction—conforming to the True Dharma and devoid of any mark of error or delusion.
Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this one-practice samādhi, they will completely fulfill all the dharmas that assist the path and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the dharma-realm as having either differentiated characteristics or a single characteristic; they swiftly attain the mark of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is inconceivable."
Within this awakening, there is likewise no attaining of Buddhahood.
One who knows thus will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
If one believes that all dharmas are entirely the Buddha-dharma, one will neither give rise to alarm nor harbor doubt.
"One who possesses such patience will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"By such causes, will one swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said,
"One attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi neither by means of causes nor by means of non-causes."
Why is this? The inconceivable realm is not attained through causes, nor is it attained through non-causes.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing such an exposition, does not give rise to indolence.
You should know that such persons have already planted various roots of goodness under previous Buddhas.
Therefore, monks and nuns who, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, do not give rise to alarm or fear, are truly those who have gone forth from the Buddha.
If an upāsaka or upāsikā hears such profound prajñāpāramitā and their mind is not startled or terrified, they have thereby accomplished a true refuge.
“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family does not practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they are not cultivating the Buddha-vehicle.”
Just as all medicinal herbs and trees grow depending upon the great earth,
Mañjuśrī, it is likewise with the bodhisattva mahāsattva: all roots of goodness increase by depending on the *prajñāpāramitā*, and they do not conflict with *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within the cities, towns, and villages of this Jambudvīpa, in what place should such a profound Prajñāpāramitā be expounded?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“In this assembly, if there are those who hear the Prajñāpāramitā and all make a vow, saying:
‘In future ages, may we always be in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā; through this faith and understanding, may we be able to hear this sūtra in future ages.’”
"You should know that this person has not come from any other minor roots of goodness, yet they are capable of receiving it and, having heard it, rejoice.
Mañjuśrī! If there is another person who hears this Prajñāpāramitā from you, you should speak thus:"
"In this Prajñāpāramitā, there are no dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or buddhas, nor are there any dharmas such as the arising and ceasing of ordinary beings."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās should come and ask me:”
"If one asks, 'How does the Tathāgata teach the Prajñāpāramitā?', I should answer:
'Since all dharmas have the characteristic of being beyond dispute, how could the Tathāgata teach the Prajñāpāramitā?'"
Why is this? Because one does not perceive any dharma that can engage in debate with another dharma, nor is there any sentient being’s consciousness capable of knowing it.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
I shall further explain the ultimate reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).
Why is this? Because the common characteristics of all dharmas equally enter into the reality-limit; for an arhat, there is no distinct or superior dharma.
Why is this? Because the dharma of an Arhat and the dharma of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) are neither identical nor different.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
When teaching the Dharma in this way, there are no sentient beings who have already attained nirvāṇa, nor those who are attaining it now, nor those who will attain it in the future.
Why is this? Because there is no determinate characteristic of a sentient being.
Mañjuśrī said: "If anyone wishes to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, I shall speak thus:
those who listen should not think of it nor be attached to it; there should be neither hearing nor attainment, just as a phantom person makes no distinctions."
To speak in this manner is the true teaching of the Dharma.

Therefore, listeners should not form dualistic conceptions; they should not cultivate the Buddha-dharma while not relinquishing their various views, nor should they grasp at the Buddha-dharma or reject the dharmas of ordinary beings.
Why is this? Because both the Buddha and ordinary beings are empty in their dualistic characteristics, as there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
If someone asks me, I shall speak thus; in this way I shall comfort them, and in this way I shall establish them.

Good sons and good daughters should inquire in this manner and abide in this manner; with minds that do not retreat or sink, they should speak in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā* according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.”
If good sons or good daughters wish to see all Buddhas, they should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
If they wish to draw near to all Buddhas and make offerings to them in accordance with the Dharma, they should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to say that the Tathāgata is my World-Honored One, one should study this Prajñāpāramitā;
if one says that the Tathāgata is not my World-Honored One, one should likewise study this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should study this *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one does not wish to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should likewise study this *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one wishes to accomplish all samādhis, one should study this Prajñāpāramitā;
if one wishes not to accomplish any samādhis, one should likewise study this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the samādhi of non-action has no distinct characteristics, and all dharmas are without arising or emergence.
If one wishes to know that all dharmas are mere designations, one should study this Prajñāpāramitā in this manner.

If one wishes to know how all sentient beings cultivate the path to enlightenment without seeking the marks of enlightenment and with a mind that never retreats or sinks, they should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because all dharmas possess the characteristic of bodhi.

If one wishes to know the characteristics of the conduct and non-conduct of all sentient beings, non-conduct is itself bodhi; bodhi is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); the dharma-realm is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). With a mind that does not retreat or sink, one should study such prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to know the supernatural transformations of all Tathāgatas—which are signless, unimpeded, and devoid of spatial location—one should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās wish not to fall into the evil realms, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.”
If one receives, maintains, reads, recites, and explains to others even a single four-line verse, in accordance with the true nature of reality,
then such sons and daughters of good family should know that they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and shall dwell in the Buddha-land.
If, upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, they are not startled or terrified, but give rise to faith and understanding, you should know that such persons are approved by the Buddha;
this is the Mahāyāna Dharma-seal practiced by the Buddha.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family studies this Dharma-seal, they will transcend the evil destinies and not enter the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, because they have transcended them.

At that time, Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven took celestial, exquisite flowers—blue lotuses (utpala), white lotuses (kumuda), white water lilies (puṇḍarīka), and celestial māndārava flowers—as well as celestial sandalwood incense, other powdered incenses, and various kinds of gold and jewels; they performed celestial music and scattered them over the Prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgatas, and Mañjuśrī as an offering.
Having made these offerings, he made this vow: "May I always hear the Dharma-seal of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Śakra Devānām-Indra further made this vow: "May the sons and daughters of good family in Jambudvīpa always be able to hear this sutra which definitively establishes the Buddha-dharma; may they all come to believe, understand, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others."
All the devas shall provide protection for them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying: “Kauśika!
"So it is, so it is! Sons and daughters of good family shall attain the definitive Bodhi of all Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If good sons and good daughters uphold [this teaching] in this manner, they will obtain great benefit and their merit will be immeasurable.
At that time, by the supernatural power of the Buddha, the entire great earth shook in six ways.
At that time, the Buddha smiled and emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"This is precisely the Tathāgata’s seal of the marks of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

So it is, so it is! When the Prajñāpāramitā has been taught, these omens all appear as a seal upon the Prajñāpāramitā, so that people may receive and uphold it, ensuring that it is neither praised nor disparaged.
Why is this? The seal of the dharma of signlessness cannot be praised or disparaged.
By means of this seal of the dharma, I now ensure that all devas and māras shall find no opportunity to gain an advantage.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly, having heard this exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
